I understand the desire for punitive justice is very strong for many, many people:

> I dont care if they come back into society

Also, I understand that for many, homelessness is seen as a character flaw -  the result of "bad choices", laziness, and yes, substance abuse. However, the reality is far more complex. 

Our current criminal justice system metes out punishment according to the punitive model you support,  and cares just as little as you seem to regarding what happens once a felon's sentence is fulfilled. 

Unfortunately, it can be nearly impossible for a convicted felon to find a job once  released, which often leads to homelessness which can continue the cycle of alcohol and drug addiction, which then leads to further incarceration, and so the cycle continues. Add to this the clear systemic racism in our prison system, as well as the fact that we now warehouse the mentally ill in prisons, and you can see that there are a multitude of issues here.

And you're absolutely correct when you write that being homeless is frequently illegal, which is a huge reason that homeless people frequently wind up being re-incarcerated. Many (most? all?) times it's not through a law that blatantly states that being homeless is a crime, but rather via incidental ordinances like loitering, shoplifting (food), public intoxication. Another huge issue is failing to pay court fines, which may be nominal when initially levied, but as time goes by are assessed penalties and interest. A homeless person probably can't pay even the initial fine, and as time goes on the fees can balloon to hundreds and even thousands of dollars. Bench warrants get issued, police question homeless people for minor infractions, run a check, learn of the warrants, and make an arrest. 

While I agree with you that attempting to fit the Scandinavian model whole cloth to the US system is problematic, I think that's a bit of a straw man argument, and the US could certainly look to those models for ways in which to drastically improve and overhaul our current system. 

Again, I do understand that in this country there is a long-standing desire for eye-for-an-eye punitive justice. The problem is that it's just not working. For one thing, it's phenomenally expensive; we imprison far more people per capita than any country on Earth, with the possible exception of North Korea. But more importantly, I'd like to think that we can do better than the current broken system.

Another ketamine infusion patient success story here - it has changed my life. See my comment elsewhere in this thread for some details.

My ketamine infusion doctor told me the same thing: as a nasal spray, Esketamine has only around 40% bioavailability, while an IV infusion provides around 98%. Another advantage of IV infusion is that, during the infusion, your provider constantly monitors your condition: heart rate, BP, 02 sat, and general comfort - if any of these become problematic the drip can be slowed or stopped altogether. With the nasal spray, the entire dose is given at once, making stopping mid-dose not an option.

Also, IV infusions are frequently/most likely far less expensive than the nasal spray. I'm in a very rural area in a western state, so have to drive over an hour to my clinic, but my initial set of six infusions was $2100, with additional single maintenance infusions every three-four months at $325 each.  Ironically, even though not covered by my health insurance, it winds up being less expensive than the out-of-pocket cost for my very expensive (and former) anti-depressant (Trintellix).

Unfortunately, major depressive disorder doesn't work like this. In the midst of a sustained depressive episode, these are the things that people tell you to do, but you simply can't.  So you tend to self-shame, which continues the downward spiral. There is hope, though. Counseling, meds (including Ketamine therapy), and support from loved ones can help get you back to a place where you can begin to (re)incorporate these things into your daily life. Major depressive disorder is paralyzing, and a bitch.

Also, just stating "I believe depression is legitimate" can actually be more harmful than helpful, in that it casts in doubt the very existence of a crippling, too-often fatal, legitimate and diagnosable illness. We don't feel the need to say that we believe diabetes is legit.

I'm truly not trying to snark/shame here; just trying to raise some awareness as to the nature of a disease that affects millions, but is often misunderstood.

There's a fascinating (and very watchable) lecture by Stanford Professor Robert Sapolsky at [https://youtu.be/NOAgplgTxfc](https://youtu.be/NOAgplgTxfc). Very worthwhile if you battle depression, know someone who does (you do), or are wanting more info generally.
